title: Measurement, classical mechanics and Newtonian gravity
scope: Pre-relativistic physics the course builds on: units and dimensional analysis, the c = 1, G = c = 1, hbar = c = 1 and Heaviside-Lorentz conventions and how to restore constants; Newton's laws, momentum and energy conservation, inertial frames, absolute space and time, and fictitious forces in accelerating and rotating frames; the calculus of variations and Lagrangian and Hamiltonian mechanics of finite-dimensional systems; Newtonian gravity as a force law and as a field (inertial, passive and active mass as definitions, potential, Gauss and Poisson laws, shell theorem, tidal tensor, escape velocity); and central-force motion with the full Kepler problem (effective potential, Binet equation, conic orbits, Kepler's laws, Laplace-Runge-Lenz vector, Bertrand's theorem). Relativistic orbits, the equivalence of the masses as a principle, field Lagrangians and Newtonian foils inside relativistic topics belong to their own domains.

concepts.title: Units and dimensional analysis
concepts.summary: Every physical quantity carries dimensions built from length, time and mass, and every term of a valid equation must share them; checking and converting units this way catches errors and fixes how constants must appear, though matching dimensions alone cannot prove an equation right.
concepts.notes: No book candidate of its own; the books use it implicitly whenever they convert units. Legacy Chapter 0 and its units lesson teach it explicitly.

concepts.title: Units with c = 1
concepts.summary: Measuring time and distance in the same unit (for example metres of light-travel time, or light-seconds) makes the speed of light the pure number 1, so velocities become fractions of c and energy, momentum and mass share one unit.
concepts.notes: Schutz ch1, Gifted Amateur ch2 and d'Inverno ch2 set only c = 1 first; the extension to G = 1 is taught later as a separate step (geometrized-units). d'Inverno arrives at it from radar ranging.

concepts.title: Geometrized units (G = c = 1)
concepts.summary: Setting both c and Newton's G to 1 turns mass, time and energy into lengths (a mass M becomes GM/c^2, about 1.5 km for the Sun), which strips G and c from relativistic formulas; results are converted back to SI only at the end.

names: geometric units with hbar and k_B retained

merged_from: geometric units with hbar and k_B retained
concepts.notes: Includes the geometrized mass m = GM/c^2 (d'Inverno ch16) and the Gifted Amateur ch28 variant that keeps hbar and k_B explicit. Schutz ch8 stresses that orbits measure GM, so geometrized masses are known far more precisely than kilogram masses.

concepts.title: Restoring factors of c and G
aliases: unit conversion rule for geometrized units
concepts.summary: To turn a geometrized formula into SI units, multiply each quantity by the power of c and G/c^2 that gives it its correct dimensions: a quantity with dimensions L^n T^m M^p becomes a length power after multiplying by c^m (G/c^2)^p, and the reverse restores the constants.
concepts.notes: Worked examples: restoring constants in G = 8 pi T gives the coupling 8 pi G/c^4 (Gifted Amateur ch0); Phi becomes Phi/c^2 in the weak-field metric (Gifted Amateur ch14).

concepts.title: Natural units (hbar = c = 1)
concepts.summary: Particle physicists set hbar and c to 1, so mass, energy and momentum carry dimensions of inverse length and any quantity reduces to a power of length; unlike geometrized units, G stays dimensional and defines the Planck scale.
concepts.notes: Gifted Amateur ch48 uses it to count length dimensions of 4D and 5D actions. Planck units themselves belong to quantum-gravity-and-beyond.

concepts.title: Heaviside-Lorentz units
concepts.summary: An electromagnetic unit system that moves the 4 pi into Coulomb's law and removes epsilon_0 and mu_0, so Maxwell's equations carry no 4 pi or material constants (div E = rho); it is often combined with c = 1 in field theory.

concepts.title: Astronomical distance units (AU, light-year, parsec)
concepts.summary: The astronomical unit is the mean Earth-Sun distance (about 1.5 x 10^11 m); the parsec is the distance at which one AU subtends one arcsecond (about 3.26 light-years), with kiloparsecs and megaparsecs used for galactic and cosmological scales.
concepts.notes: Gifted Amateur ch0 introduces the AU inside the Sun-mass estimate; Gifted Amateur ch15 and d'Inverno ch26 introduce parsecs to give H0 its units.

concepts.title: Absolute time
concepts.summary: Newtonian physics assumes a single universal time: once synchronized, every observer's clock agrees on when any event happens, so there is one shared present moment and simultaneity is the same for everyone.
concepts.notes: In the Galilean transformation it appears as t' = t. Gifted Amateur ch1 draws it as a horizontal "now" slice later replaced by the light cone.

concepts.title: Newton's first law
concepts.summary: A body acted on by no net force stays at rest or keeps moving in a straight line at constant speed; the law is really a statement that frames exist (inertial frames) in which this is true.
concepts.notes: Gifted Amateur ch2 recovers it from the free-particle Lagrangian and restates it as constant 4-velocity.

concepts.title: Inertial frame
concepts.summary: A frame of reference in which a force-free body moves uniformly in a straight line, so Newton's laws hold in their simple form; any two inertial frames move uniformly relative to each other, and acceleration (unlike uniform velocity) is detectable from inside a system.

names: absoluteness of acceleration in Newtonian mechanics

merged_from: absoluteness of acceleration in Newtonian mechanics
concepts.notes: Includes Schutz ch1's point that acceleration is absolute in Newtonian mechanics (soup climbing the bowl on an accelerating train). How the universe selects inertial frames (bucket, distant stars, Mach) belongs to equivalence-principle.

concepts.title: Absolute space
concepts.summary: Newton postulated an immovable background space against which all motion is ultimately measured; inertial observers are those at rest or moving uniformly relative to it, and inertial forces signal acceleration relative to it.

concepts.title: Inertial mass
concepts.summary: Inertial mass measures how strongly a body resists changes in its motion; operationally, when two isolated bodies push on each other, the ratio of their masses is the inverse ratio of their accelerations, which lets one calibrate any mass against a standard.

names: operational measurement of mass by mutual accelerations

merged_from: operational measurement of mass by mutual accelerations
concepts.notes: Includes d'Inverno ch4's operational calibration by mutual accelerations (which uses the second and third laws). A priori inertial mass has nothing to do with gravity; its equality with gravitational mass belongs to equivalence-principle.

concepts.title: Linear momentum
concepts.summary: The linear momentum of a body is its mass times its velocity, p = m v, and the momentum of a system is the vector sum over its parts; it is the quantity whose rate of change Newton's second law equates to force.

concepts.title: Force
concepts.summary: Force is what changes a body's momentum; within Newtonian mechanics it is measured through F = dp/dt, so it gains independent physical content only through separate force laws (such as gravitation) and the action-reaction property.

names: operational status of force in Newtonian mechanics

merged_from: operational status of force in Newtonian mechanics
concepts.notes: Folds in d'Inverno ch4's discussion of the apparent circularity of defining force and mass through the laws themselves.

concepts.title: Newton's second law
concepts.summary: The net force on a body equals the rate of change of its momentum, F = dp/dt, which reduces to F = m a when the mass is constant; given the forces and initial position and velocity, it predicts the whole motion.
concepts.notes: The momentum form is the one that survives in relativity. Legacy Chapter 0 stresses that a second-order law needs two initial data.

concepts.title: Newton's third law
concepts.summary: When two bodies interact, the force on the first due to the second is equal in size and opposite in direction to the force on the second due to the first, F_ij = -F_ji.

concepts.title: Conservation of linear momentum
concepts.summary: For an isolated system, on which no net external force acts, internal forces cancel in action-reaction pairs, so the total momentum stays constant through any interaction.
concepts.notes: Includes the definitions of internal versus external forces and of an isolated (closed) system used in the proof (d'Inverno ch4).

concepts.title: Conservative force and potential energy
concepts.summary: A force field is conservative when the work it does around every closed path is zero; it can then be written as minus the gradient of a potential energy, F = -grad U, whose zero point is arbitrary.

concepts.title: Conservation of mechanical energy
concepts.summary: The work done by the net force equals the change in kinetic energy (1/2) m v^2; when all forces are conservative this makes kinetic plus potential energy constant along the motion.
concepts.notes: No book candidate of its own; the books use it throughout (escape velocity, orbits). Legacy Chapter 0 and its mechanics-energy lesson teach it.

concepts.title: Inertial (fictitious) force
concepts.summary: When Newton's second law is written with accelerations measured in a non-inertial frame, extra force terms proportional to the body's mass appear (for a linearly accelerating frame, -m a); in curvilinear or accelerated coordinates these are exactly the connection terms of the equation of motion.
concepts.notes: Gifted Amateur ch8 reinterprets it as the Christoffel term moved to the force side; d'Inverno ch9 uses it to pose the question of the physical origin of inertia.

concepts.title: Centrifugal and Coriolis forces
concepts.summary: In a frame rotating with angular velocity omega, a body appears to feel an outward centrifugal force -m omega x (omega x r), a velocity-dependent Coriolis force -2m omega x v, and an Euler force -m (d omega/dt) x r if the rotation rate changes.
concepts.notes: Example: the swingball of Gifted Amateur ch8. Gifted Amateur ch3 shows the Minkowski line element in rotating coordinates acquiring cross terms, a preview of how coordinates complicate a simple law.

concepts.title: Driven damped harmonic oscillator and resonance
concepts.summary: A damped oscillator driven sinusoidally settles into steady oscillation at the driving frequency, with an amplitude that peaks when the drive matches the natural frequency and a peak height inversely proportional to the damping.
concepts.notes: d'Inverno ch21 uses it for a resonant bar driven by a gravitational wave.

concepts.title: Range of validity of Newtonian physics
concepts.summary: A physical theory is trusted only within the regimes where it matches experiment; Newtonian mechanics and gravity are excellent for speeds far below c and weak potentials (|Phi|/c^2 much less than 1), and relativity refines rather than refutes them there.

concepts.title: Generalized coordinates
concepts.summary: Any set of independent variables q^a that fixes a system's configuration, together with their time derivatives (generalized velocities) and the generalized forces -dV/dq^a, can describe its motion; the choice is free and adapted to the problem.

concepts.title: Calculus of variations
concepts.summary: The calculus of variations finds the functions that make an integral of F(y, y', x) stationary: perturb the function by a small variation that vanishes at the fixed endpoints and demand that the first-order change of the integral be zero; the stationary point can be a minimum, maximum or saddle.
concepts.notes: Folds in d'Inverno ch7's definition of the variation delta y = epsilon eta(x). Canonical example: the shortest path in the plane is a straight line (Gifted Amateur ch1).

concepts.title: Fundamental lemma of the calculus of variations
concepts.summary: If a continuous function integrates to zero against every smooth test function that vanishes at the endpoints, the function itself must vanish everywhere; this is the step that turns a vanishing first variation into a differential equation.

names: fundamental lemma of the calculus of variations
fundamental lemma of the calculus of variations
fundamental lemma of calculus of variations

merged_from: fundamental lemma of the calculus of variations
concepts.notes: d'Inverno ch7 proves it with a polynomial bump; d'Inverno ch11 reuses it (and its vector version) to extract the field equations.

concepts.title: Euler-Lagrange equation
concepts.summary: A path makes the integral of L(q, dq/dt, t) stationary with fixed endpoints exactly when d/dt(dL/d q-dot) = dL/dq, with one such equation for each independent coordinate.

names: Euler-Lagrange equations for several dependent variables

merged_from: Euler-Lagrange equations for several dependent variables
concepts.notes: Derived by integration by parts and the vanishing boundary term. The several-variable version (d'Inverno ch7) is folded in.

concepts.title: Lagrangian
concepts.summary: The Lagrangian is a function of generalized coordinates, velocities and time whose time integral is the action; for Newtonian systems it is kinetic minus potential energy, L = T - V, and multiplying it by a constant or adding a constant leaves the equations of motion unchanged.
concepts.notes: Folds in d'Inverno ch8's remark on equivalent Lagrangians (constant rescaling and shifts; for geodesic Lagrangians also L^2 versus L^(1/2)).

concepts.title: Hamilton's principle
concepts.summary: Among all paths between fixed initial and final configurations, a mechanical system follows one for which the action S = integral of L dt is stationary; the usual name "least action" is misleading because the stationary point may be a saddle or maximum.
concepts.notes: Covers the action as a number assigned to each path in particle mechanics. Gifted Amateur ch8 uses the saddle/maximum possibility to motivate maximal proper time. The field-theory form belongs to action-principles-and-field-theory.

concepts.title: Canonical (conjugate) momentum
concepts.summary: The momentum conjugate to a generalized coordinate is p_a = dL/d(q-dot^a); for a free particle it is ordinary momentum, and because it differentiates with respect to a velocity component it naturally carries a lower index.

concepts.title: Cyclic (ignorable) coordinate
concepts.summary: If a Lagrangian does not depend on some coordinate, the Euler-Lagrange equation for that coordinate says its conjugate momentum is conserved; for motion in a central potential the angle is cyclic, giving conserved angular momentum.
concepts.notes: Taught in the Newtonian setting through the polar Lagrangian of the Kepler problem (Gifted Amateur ch20). The relativistic use with metric symmetries belongs to geodesics-and-symmetries.

concepts.title: Constant of the motion
concepts.summary: A constant of the motion is a quantity that keeps the same value along every trajectory, such as energy or angular momentum; each one lowers the order of the equations that must be integrated, which is why symmetric problems are solvable.

concepts.title: Hamiltonian
concepts.summary: The Hamiltonian is the Legendre transform of the Lagrangian, H = p_a q-dot^a - L, expressed in coordinates and momenta; when it has no explicit time dependence it is conserved and, for ordinary mechanical systems, equals the total energy.
concepts.notes: Example: for the geodesic Lagrangian the Hamiltonian is (1/2) g^{mu nu} p_mu p_nu (Gifted Amateur ch40). d'Inverno ch8 uses it to obtain relativistic energy. The field Hamiltonian density belongs to action-principles-and-field-theory.

concepts.title: Hamilton's equations and phase space
concepts.summary: Hamilton's equations dq/dt = dH/dp and dp/dt = -dH/dq replace one second-order equation per coordinate with two first-order ones, so a state is a point in phase space (q, p) that flows along curves of constant energy.
concepts.notes: Gifted Amateur ch40 exercises re-derive geodesics from Hamilton's equations. The legacy course has a spring-cart phase-space lab and section on Poisson brackets.

concepts.title: Hamilton-Jacobi equation
concepts.summary: Classical mechanics can be rewritten as one partial differential equation for Hamilton's principal function S, with H + dS/dt = 0 and momenta given by the gradient of S; its surfaces of constant S behave like wavefronts and are the classical limit of quantum phases.
concepts.notes: Only mentioned (Gifted Amateur ch49) to explain the kinship between classical action and quantum phase.

concepts.title: Newton's law of universal gravitation
concepts.summary: Any two point masses attract along the line joining them with a force of magnitude G M m / r^2, where G is about 6.67 x 10^-11 N m^2 kg^-2; the same law governs falling apples and the orbiting Moon.
concepts.notes: Folds in the gravitational constant G. Schutz ch7 frames Newtonian gravity as two laws (force from potential, potential from density) that a relativistic theory must generalize.

concepts.title: Action at a distance
concepts.summary: In Newton's theory one mass affects another instantly across empty space with no mechanism or propagation delay, which requires a universal simultaneity that special relativity denies and so demands a new theory of gravity.

concepts.title: Cavendish experiment
concepts.summary: Cavendish's 1798 torsion balance measured the tiny attraction between lead spheres, fixing G and so letting the Earth's mass and mean density be deduced from surface gravity.

concepts.title: Newtonian gravitational field
concepts.summary: The gravitational field g(x) is the gravitational force per unit test mass at each point: radially inward with magnitude GM/r^2 for a point mass, and an integral over the density for an extended source.

concepts.title: Newtonian gravitational potential
concepts.summary: Because the gravitational field is conservative it can be written g = -grad Phi, with Phi = -GM/r for a point mass (potential energy -GMm/r); by superposition, any distribution gives Phi = -G times the integral of rho/|x - x'|.
concepts.notes: Folds in the potential energy U = -GMm/r and the superposition (linearity) of Newtonian gravity. Phi has dimensions of velocity squared, so Phi/c^2 measures field strength.

concepts.title: Passive gravitational mass
concepts.summary: Passive gravitational mass measures how strongly a body responds to an external gravitational field, through F = -m^P grad phi; unlike inertial mass, it is tied to gravity by definition.
concepts.notes: d'Inverno ch9 separates inertial, passive and active masses. Their equality as a principle, and its tests, belong to equivalence-principle.

concepts.title: Active gravitational mass
concepts.summary: Active gravitational mass measures how strong a gravitational field a body produces, through phi = -G m^A / r for a point source; Newton's third law applied to two attracting bodies forces it to be proportional to passive mass.
concepts.notes: The relativistic generalization (rho + 3p as the source, Schutz ch8) belongs to einstein-field-equations.

concepts.title: Gauss's law for gravity
concepts.summary: The outward flux of the gravitational field through any closed surface equals -4 pi G times the mass enclosed; in differential form, div g = -4 pi G rho.

concepts.title: Newton's shell theorem
concepts.summary: Outside a spherically symmetric mass distribution the field and potential are exactly those of a point with the same total mass at the centre, which justifies treating planets and stars as point masses.

concepts.title: Poisson equation for gravity
concepts.summary: The field equation of Newtonian gravity is nabla^2 Phi = 4 pi G rho: two spatial derivatives of the potential are set by the local mass density, reducing to Laplace's equation in empty space; it is the template the Einstein equation must reproduce.

names: Poisson's equation for the gravitational potential

merged_from: Poisson's equation for the gravitational potential
concepts.notes: Derived either from Gauss's law or by taking the Laplacian of the integral potential using nabla^2(1/r) = -4 pi delta^3. Point-mass solution phi = -Gm/r (Schutz ch8 exercise).

concepts.title: Newtonian tidal tensor
concepts.summary: The matrix of second derivatives of the Newtonian potential, d^2 Phi/dx^i dx^j, gives the relative acceleration of two nearby freely falling particles, d^2 s^i/dt^2 = -(d_i d_j Phi) s^j; for a point mass it stretches along the radius and squeezes sideways, and outside matter its trace vanishes.
concepts.notes: Example: for a point mass on the z-axis it is (GM/z^3) diag(1, 1, -2). Its trace equals 4 pi G rho by Poisson's equation, the hook used to guess the Einstein equation.

concepts.title: Escape velocity
concepts.summary: The minimum launch speed that lets a projectile coast to infinity is found by setting kinetic plus gravitational potential energy to zero: v_esc = sqrt(2GM/r).
concepts.notes: Setting v_esc = c gives the Michell-Laplace dark-star radius 2GM/c^2. Gifted Amateur ch6 reads the gravitational time-dilation factor as the gamma factor of the escape speed.

concepts.title: Gravity as the dominant long-range interaction
concepts.summary: Gravity is by far the weakest fundamental interaction, but it has infinite range and ordinary matter only attracts, so contributions add without cancelling, while electric charges neutralize; that is why gravity governs planets, galaxies and the universe.

names: gravity as the dominant long-range interaction

merged_from: gravity as the dominant long-range interaction

concepts.title: Central force
concepts.summary: A central force always points along the line to a fixed centre and depends only on the distance r from it; Newtonian gravity of a fixed mass, F = -GMm r/r^3, is the prime example.

concepts.title: Conservation of angular momentum in central-force motion
concepts.summary: A central force exerts no torque about the centre, so the angular momentum L = r x p is constant in size and direction; the motion stays in a fixed plane and r^2 dphi/dt = h is constant.

names: Conservation of angular momentum in central-force motion

merged_from: Conservation of angular momentum in central-force motion

concepts.title: Kepler's second law
concepts.summary: The line from the Sun to a planet sweeps out equal areas in equal times; the areal velocity dA/dt = r^2 (dphi/dt)/2 = L/(2m) is constant for any central force, so this law is angular momentum conservation in disguise.

concepts.title: Two-body problem and reduced mass
concepts.summary: Two bodies attracting each other can be separated into free motion of their centre of mass and the relative motion of one fictitious body of reduced mass m1 m2/(m1 + m2) in the inverse-square field of the total mass.

names: Reduced mass and the two-body problem

merged_from: Reduced mass and the two-body problem
concepts.notes: d'Inverno ch21 uses it to set up a Newtonian binary as a gravitational-wave source.

concepts.title: Kepler problem
aliases: one-body problem in an inverse-square field
concepts.summary: The Kepler problem asks for every trajectory of a particle moving under an attractive inverse-square force from a fixed centre; writing L = (1/2) m (r-dot^2 + r^2 phi-dot^2) + GMm/r gives the radial and angular equations whose solutions are conic sections with the centre at a focus.
concepts.notes: Folds in the polar Lagrangian of Gifted Amateur ch20. d'Inverno ch16 reviews it as the baseline for the relativistic orbit equation.

concepts.title: Newtonian effective potential
concepts.summary: With angular momentum conserved, the radial motion obeys E = (1/2) m r-dot^2 + U_eff(r) with U_eff = L^2/(2 m r^2) - GMm/r, a one-dimensional problem read off graphically: turning points where E = U_eff, a centrifugal barrier at small r, and a stable circular orbit at the minimum.

names: stability of circular orbits in power-law forces

merged_from: stability of circular orbits in power-law forces
concepts.notes: Folds in the Newtonian turning points, angular-momentum barrier and circular orbit (E = -GMm/(2 r0)). Example: for power-law forces F = -A r^n a stable circular orbit exists only if n > -3 (Gifted Amateur ch20).

concepts.title: Binet equation
concepts.summary: Using u = 1/r as the unknown and the angle as the independent variable turns the radial equation of central-force motion into d^2u/dphi^2 + u = GM/h^2 for gravity, a shifted harmonic oscillator whose solutions u = u0 + B cos phi are the orbits.
concepts.notes: Reused (often as u = M/r) for relativistic orbits and light bending in Gifted Amateur ch23-24.

concepts.title: Conic-section solutions of the Kepler problem
concepts.summary: Every trajectory in an attractive inverse-square field is a conic with the centre of force at a focus, l/r = 1 + e cos(phi - phi0), where the semi-latus rectum l = h^2/(GM) sets the size, e the shape and phi0 the direction of perihelion.

names: conic-section solutions of the Kepler problem

merged_from: conic-section solutions of the Kepler problem

concepts.title: Orbital eccentricity
concepts.summary: Eccentricity is the dimensionless shape parameter of a conic orbit: 0 for a circle, between 0 and 1 for an ellipse, 1 for a parabola and above 1 for a hyperbola; for a Kepler orbit it is fixed by energy and angular momentum through e^2 = 1 + 2 E L^2/(G^2 M^2 m^3).
concepts.notes: Gifted Amateur ch23 redefines it relativistically so that it reduces to the Newtonian value in the weak-field limit.

concepts.title: Geometry of an elliptical orbit
concepts.summary: An elliptical orbit has semi-major axis a, semi-minor axis b = a sqrt(1 - e^2), area pi a b and a focus at distance e a from the centre; its closest and farthest points (apsides: perihelion and aphelion, periapsis and apoapsis in general) lie on the major axis, and L^2 = G M m^2 a (1 - e^2).

names: angular momentum of an elliptical orbit

merged_from: angular momentum of an elliptical orbit
concepts.notes: Folds in the vocabulary of apsides (warning that "perihelion" strictly refers to the Sun) and the angular momentum of an elliptical orbit.

concepts.title: Kepler's first law
concepts.summary: Bound planetary orbits are ellipses with the Sun at one focus; found empirically by Kepler, it follows as the negative-energy solution of the inverse-square orbit equation.

concepts.title: Kepler's third law
concepts.summary: The square of the orbital period is proportional to the cube of the semi-major axis, T^2 = 4 pi^2 a^3/(GM); for two bodies M is the total mass, so a circular binary of separation a has angular frequency Omega^2 = G(m1 + m2)/a^3.

names: Kepler's third law for a circular binary

merged_from: Kepler's third law for a circular binary
concepts.notes: Folds in the circular-binary form used for gravitational-wave sources (d'Inverno ch21).

concepts.title: Bound and unbound orbits
concepts.summary: The sign of the total energy classifies Kepler trajectories: E < 0 gives bound ellipses (circles as the special case), E = 0 the marginally unbound parabola, and E > 0 hyperbolic fly-bys that approach once and escape to infinity.

concepts.title: Energy of a Kepler orbit
concepts.summary: The total energy of a bound Kepler orbit depends only on its semi-major axis, E = -GMm/(2a); because it is negative, a system that loses energy (for example to gravitational waves) moves to a tighter orbit and speeds up.
concepts.notes: Folds in Gifted Amateur ch46's explanation of why a radiating binary spins up.

concepts.title: Negative specific heat of self-gravitating systems
concepts.summary: A bound self-gravitating system that loses energy contracts and its particles move faster, so it heats up as it cools; this negative heat capacity makes such systems thermodynamically unstable and drives stellar cores to contract and heat after fuel runs out.

names: negative specific heat of self-gravitating systems

merged_from: negative specific heat of self-gravitating systems
concepts.notes: Schutz ch10 asserts it; the virial theorem (E = -K) is the natural justification.

concepts.title: Laplace-Runge-Lenz vector
concepts.summary: For the inverse-square force the vector p x L - G M m^2 r/r is conserved; it points from the focus to perihelion with size proportional to the eccentricity, so its constancy means Newtonian orbits close and their perihelion does not move.

names: constants of the motion and superintegrability

merged_from: constants of the motion and superintegrability
concepts.notes: Folds in the superintegrability count: with 3 degrees of freedom at most 5 independent constants exist, and E, L and the LRL vector supply all 5.

concepts.title: Bertrand's theorem
concepts.summary: Among central forces, only the inverse-square law and the linear (harmonic) force make every bounded orbit close on itself, so any deviation from 1/r^2, relativistic or otherwise, makes orbits precess.
concepts.notes: Gifted Amateur ch20 contains only its near-circular content, without the name.

out_of_scope_candidates.name: compactness parameter
out_of_scope_candidates.note: Same idea as the relativistic strength parameter |Phi|/c^2 (GM/c^2 r) that equivalence-principle owns.

out_of_scope_candidates.name: effective potential
out_of_scope_candidates.note: Schutz ch11 effective potential V^2(r) is the Schwarzschild effective potential; the Newtonian version is newtonian-effective-potential here.

out_of_scope_candidates.name: Newtonian hydrostatic equilibrium
out_of_scope_candidates.note: Newtonian hydrostatics belongs to matter-and-stress-energy; it appears here only as the leading factor of the TOV equation.

out_of_scope_candidates.name: active gravitational mass (rho + 3p, Schutz ch08)
out_of_scope_candidates.note: Only the Newtonian definition (d'Inverno ch9) is taken here as active-gravitational-mass.

out_of_scope_candidates.name: Hamiltonian density
out_of_scope_candidates.note: Gifted Amateur ch40 cluster also treats the particle Hamiltonian, which is taken here.
